slides.text: This video is a general guide to the final project, worth thirty percent of the course and mapped to all four outcomes. Always follow the brief and rubric from your instructor. This guide shows how to turn everything you learned into one clear project and presentation.

The final project is a summative project that shows the whole pipeline on one dataset. It tests all four outcomes: analysing the dataset, applying univariate, bivariate and multivariate E D A, cleaning and transforming it, and interpreting results into insights that support hypotheses. Resources include datasets and case studies from domains like insurance, retail, pharma and healthcare.

Choose a dataset and a question. Pick a real dataset from a domain you can explain, such as insurance, retail, pharma or healthcare. It should have enough rows, a target or outcome you care about, and some real mess: missing values, outliers, categories. Write the problem statement, the unit of observation, and the sentence: this sample can support claims about, blank, and cannot support claims about, blank.

Structure the project like an industry notebook. Title block and executive summary. Problem, target and success metric. Refined hypotheses. Setup with a single seed and versions. Data audit. E D A to insights. Stratified split. Pipeline with cross-validation. Test set used once. Insights and recommendations. Limitations and next steps. And a submission checklist.

State clearly, for every headline claim, whether it is exploratory, generated by this analysis, or confirmatory, pre-specified before you looked. Explore on the training part and confirm only on held-out rows. If you test many things on one dataset, correct for multiple testing. This honesty is part of what makes the project trustworthy.

Prepare the data carefully. Audit and fix quality problems with a log. Explain missing values before imputing and compare methods. Treat outliers by cause. Encode categories by type. Transform skewed columns, and consider feature engineering and dimension reduction if they help. Put every step that learns from data inside a pipeline fitted on training rows only, to avoid leakage.

Present a story. Context: what situation is this and why does it matter. Conflict: what did the data reveal that is surprising or wrong. Resolution: what do you recommend and what will change. Use an insight title on each slide, honest axes, one chart per message, and turn each insight into observation, evidence, meaning and action that a manager could use without reading your code.

Check yourself before presenting. Is the problem and metric clear? Is every claim labelled? Is the data audited and the cleaning logged? Are charts honest? Is the model evaluated on a test set used once? Can you answer why you chose each method? Does the project state its limits? And does the notebook run from top to bottom with no errors?

A few last tips. Keep the project focused: one question, done well, beats many half-finished ones. Practise the presentation with a timer. Be ready to explain any number, any chart and any choice. And ask for feedback early. Good luck with your final project, and thanks for watching.
